en: Sādhanamālā 239: Mahāmāyāsādhana by Ratnākaraśānti [NGMPP B 24/12, DSCN9071 = 986 ff.]
I bow to the one named Mahāmāya, who has four faces and four arms,
upon whose lap sits the Goddess, and who has other goddesses in the four directions.
Out of compassion for Mahāvajradhara himself, who possesses a terrifying form,
the *sādhana* of the one known as Mahāmāya is now properly explained.

In this regard, the practitioner (mantrin) authorized for cultivation, awakened by the exhortation of the songs of the four goddesses, should rise in the morning and, having purified himself with rays from the syllable *hūṃ* situated upon the sun in his own heart, perform the cleansing of his mouth and so forth. Having established the protection of the site, himself, and the yoga with the mantra *hūṃ phaṭ*, he enters the meditation chamber. After consecrating the water offering (*argha*) with the syllable *hūṃ*, he sits in a comfortable posture. Beholding the Blessed One together with his retinue in the sky before him, he worships them with clouds of the five offerings arising from the rays of the heart-mantra, and should perform the confession of misdeeds and so forth.

I confess my own sins; I rejoice in all the merits of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, noble ones, and ordinary beings; I dedicate all my own roots of virtue toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; and until I reach awakening, I go for refuge to the Three Jewels: the Jewel of the Buddha, the Jewel of the Dharma, and the Jewel of the Saṅgha.

"O, may I indeed attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment for the sake and welfare of all sentient beings, until they are established in ultimate, final nirvana and in the unsurpassed wisdom of a Tathāgata."

Thereafter, one should resolve that all this is indeed mind-only (*cittamātra*), appearing in various unreal forms just like a dream; having abandoned all forms, one should perceive a mere luminosity that is infinite, free from appearances, and resembling the stainless sky. One should then consecrate oneself with: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham* ("I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness").

Immediately thereafter, having visualized a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) in the sky before one through the syllable *hūṃ*, and by means of the expansion of its blazing rays, one should contemplate a ground made of vajras below, a vajra-fence (*vajraprākāra*) across, a vajra-canopy (*vajrapañjara*) above, and in the center, a fearsome cremation ground (*ghoraśmaśāna*). In the middle of that, one should see a single-chambered gabled temple (*kūṭāgāra*) composed of all kinds of jewels;
it is square, with four doors, adorned with four archways (*toraṇa*), and possesses four radiant altars with necklaces and other ornaments, as well as celestial nymphs (*apsaras*).

Having meditated upon an eight-petaled red lotus in the center of that, one should meditate upon the drop of the nectar of gnosis—without beginning or end, resembling a pearl of the *tāra* syllable—within its pericarp;
this is the first samādhi, called the "Initial Yoga."

From the central bindu itself, one should visualize four bindus radiating out to the petals of the directions, which transform into seed-syllables: *hūṃ*, *svā*, *āḥ*, and *hāḥ*. From these, in their respective order, one should emanate the lords of the Vajra, Jewel, Lotus, and Action families, along with their respective families; then, having reabsorbed them back into those very same syllables, one should visualize the four Yoginīs transformed from them.

On the eastern petal is Vajraḍākinī, blue in color, with faces that are blue, yellow, white, and green; she holds a vajra, a skull-cup, a bell, and a khaṭvāṅga. On the southern petal is Ratnaḍākinī, yellow in color, with faces that are yellow, blue, white, and green; she holds a jewel-tassel, a trident, and a banner of a jackal held at her neck. On the western petal is Padmaḍākinī, white in color, with faces that are white, yellow, blue, and green; she holds a universal lotus, an arrow, a skull-cup, and a bow. On the northern petal is Viśvaḍākinī, green in color, with faces that are green, yellow, white, and blue; she holds a sword, a ḍamaru drum, a noose, and a skull-cup.
All of them, possessing the splendor of moon-seats, should rouse their Lord from his remainder [of sleep] with this vajra-song, just as they do for the Master.
O friend! The lotus of youth has been awakened by the lute;
alas, alas, alas! It has been propitiated with great joy through dancing.
The lotus has blossomed by the rays of the sun with great joy;
Alalalala! Ho! It has been propitiated and danced with great joy.

Then, by the power of the song, the Blessed One, having abandoned his form as a drop (*bindu*), manifests in the shape of two seed-syllables: *oṃ* and *hūṃ*. Then, from the syllable *oṃ*, one should emanate Vairocana and his family, and subsequently reabsorb them; from the syllable *hūṃ*, the five Jinas and their families. Thereafter, together with the Buddha-Ḍākinī produced from the syllable *oṃ*, the Blessed Lord Heruka arises from the syllable *hūṃ*.
Kṛṣṇa is smeared with ashes, possessing the splendor of a seat of shimmering suns;
his tawny hair blazes upward, and he is formidable with a crown of skulls.
He has four faces— blue, yellow, great white, and green—
and four arms, holding a skull-cup, an arrow, a khaṭvāṅga staff, and a bow.
Through the purification of the five Buddhas, he is adorned with the five mudrās:
the wheel on the head, the earrings, the necklace, the bracelet on the hand, and the girdle.
Clad in human skin, with twelve blood-red eyes,
surrounded by garlands of flames, beautiful through the supreme bliss of wrath,
he stands in the dance posture of half-lotus, endowed with the nine sentiments of drama.
She performs the welfare of the world through multitudes of Victors who emit infinite rays of light;
she is red, her two arms—clad in weapons equal to her beloved—are embracing his neck.
The illustrious Buddhaḍākinī has red, yellow, white, and green faces;
she is the Śavarī who receives the empowerment from the Buddhas, as she is described in the Hevajra Tantra.
Likewise, here the Buddha-Ḍākinī is joined with Heruka;
he is called "Buddha" because he delights sentient beings through the Buddha-body.

"Pure phenomena by nature"—this is the whiteness of Vāgīśvara himself. Thereafter, one should contemplate the syllable Oṃ, red, at the Blessed One’s faculty of sight; the syllable Hūṃ, blue, at the faculty of hearing; the syllable Cī, yellow, at the faculty of smell; the syllable Āḥ, white, at the faculty of taste; the syllable Re, green, at the location of the uṣṇīṣa; and the syllable Khe, white, in the mind. This is the armor consisting of the placement of the six syllables upon the six faculties. Then, the empowerment of body, speech, and mind with Oṃ, Āḥ, and Hūṃ is performed respectively on the head, throat, and heart.

Having visualized the seed-syllable of one’s own deity within the sun between the breasts, which has the nature of that very gnosis, one should draw in the mandala of gnosis with the hooks of its rays; having dispelled obstacles with the syllable *hūṃ*, offered the water for honor (*argha*), and [uttered] *jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ* to attract, cause entry, bind, and subjugate, one should behold the pledge-mandala (*samayamaṇḍala*) as having become one with it in a single fusion.

Then, five yoginīs dispatched by the Tathāgatas, impelled by the rays of light from the seed-syllable of gnosis (*jñānabīja*), arrive and consecrate the Blessed One and the yoginīs with precious vases filled with the water of the five gnoses. As they are being consecrated, the Lord of their respective families arises upon their heads: for the Blessed One it is Akṣobhya; for Buddhaḍākinī and the others, in due order, they are Śāśvata, Akṣobhya, Ratneśa, Vāgīśa, and Amoghasiddhi. Then, one should worship the Blessed One and the Blessed Lady with offerings of the five types of service and the five qualities of sensory pleasure, emanated through the mouths of the rays of light from the seed-syllable of gnosis.
Then one should praise the Blessed One through the mouths of the goddesses:
"I bow to Śrī Heruka, who is adorned with a garland of mantras and a string of skulls, most terrible with his protruding fangs, and devouring great flesh."
Then, through the yoga of radiation, the goddesses of the directions should merge into the Buddha-Ḍākinī.

Then, having visualized upon her head, heart, navel, secret place, and thighs the syllables OṂ HŪṂ SVĀ ĀḤ HĀ respectively, one should cause her body to be pervaded by these [syllables] radiating back and forth until they meet one another. By means of that [consort], who possesses a red lotus born from the syllable HRĪḤ with a pericarp born from the syllable A, and likewise a vajra born from the syllable HŪṂ and a jewel born from the syllable OṂ, one should begin the sexual union with this mantra: *anurāgayāmi* ("I cause [her] to be impassioned").

Then, impelled by the rays of light from the two jewels, the Tathāgatas arrive, enter through the mouth, dissolve, and fall into the interior of the lotus. One should contemplate that nectar of the five gnoses being received with playful grace upon the tip of the tongue;
this is the second samādhi, named Maṇḍalarājāgrī.

Then, impelled by the Blessed One, the Buddha-Ḍākinīs and others—the five in each of the five [families]—for the sake of sentient beings, through the radiation of clouds of bodies from the Blessed One, sequentially generated the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), the wisdom of the perfectly pure realm of phenomena (*suviśuddhadharmadhātujñāna*), the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*), the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣājñāna*), the wisdom of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*), and the state of the Great Vajradhara; they then reabsorbed their own clouds of bodies into the root body.
This is the third meditative absorption, named "The Supreme King of Activities" (*karmarājāgrī*).

If, moreover, the yogin should wish to stabilize the mind for the sake of accomplishing the foremost of all meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), then, in brief, having visualized the three meditative absorptions, he should contemplate a union of sun and moon at the pericarp of the navel-lotus, seamless at its edges. In its center, he should conceive of the Hero, who consists of great bliss, as a drop (*bindu*)—subtle as a mustard seed, white, clear, and the nature of gnosis (*jñāna*). From him, a line of light rays, resembling a lotus fiber, emerges through the center of the moon and encircles the union three times transversely.
Having seen her standing with her senses restrained, one should visualize sixteen syllables each, strung together upon the three half-coils situated above the moon.
For it is said in the *Samvarottara*:
"One should arrange the letters from *ka* to *da*, excluding *ṅa* and *ña*."

One should draw the two *ālis* (vowel and consonant series) beginning with the letter *dha* and ending with the letter *ha*. The *āli* of the vowel *a* should be placed in the center as the lunar mandala.
Here too it is said: "divine by means of rows of syllables."

Thus, meditating on the Hero within the womb of the union of the sun and moon at the pericarp of the navel-lotus, and being intent upon the ripening of that meditation, one should perceive from that very place a second subtle line of light rays, standing like a single blazing flame.

By its power, the Hero is flooded by a flowing torrent of nectar, and that line of light rays becomes cool. Then, with the mind fixed upon the Hero, one should gaze upon it until one perceives through signs the attainment of stability of mind.

Once stability has been observed, one should clearly contemplate that line of rays as illuminating the infinite universe with light; then, seeing everything like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand, one should swiftly accomplish all meditative absorptions (samādhis).
This is the *binduyoga*. ||o||

Success belongs to one who has recited the vidyā; thus, "recitation" (japa) is explained. In the same way, the yogin of the wheel of the six deities should visualize the Hero within the interior of the union of the sun and moon situated at the pericarp of the navel-lotus. Likewise, he should recite the mantra within that union, which is encircled by three coils and bound by a line of rays consisting of three rows of syllables.

In this tantra, the mantras consist of three syllables. Among them, the mantra of the Blessed One is *oṃ hūṃ hūṃ*. The mantras of Buddhaḍākinī and the others, in their respective order, are: *oṃ oṃ huṃ*, *oṃ huṃ huṃ*, *oṃ svā hūṃ*, *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*, and *oṃ hā hūṃ*.

How should one recite? Having placed the seed-syllable to be recited within the interior of the *saṃpuṭa*, and having raised the Hero (*vīra*) above its head while uttering the syllable *oṃ*, one should raise a line of light rays from the Hero together with the breath-wind and, illuminating [the world] with that, make the world consist of Buddhas.

While uttering the seed-syllable, one should resolve that all those Buddhas have the nature of one's own deity. While uttering the internal *hūṃ*, one should draw back that world consisting of Buddhas by means of the exhalation-wind and dissolve it into the Hero. One should do this again and again until fatigue occurs.

When fatigued, one should rest; then, having dedicated all this merit toward unexcelled perfect enlightenment and the attainment of the desired fruit, one should perform worship as before, dissolve the maṇḍala into the seed-syllable at one's own heart, and rising from that, resolve that oneself is of the nature of one's own deity, and perform everything [else].

Having made all food consist of the nectar of the five gnoses by means of the five seeds, and having visualized and contemplated the circle of deities within one’s own heart, one should offer that nectar into their tongues. While bathing, one should meditate on the ritual of the consecration of the deities.

At the junctions of midday and evening twilight, however, one should enter the maṇḍala house and, having emanated the foundational maṇḍala by means of the rays from the seed-syllable in one's own heart, emanate the four yoginīs in succession from that very seed-syllable and settle them in their respective places. Having performed the entire ritual procedure, such as the consecration and so forth, as before, and having dissolved the maṇḍala within, one should then arise and perform the yoga of meditative absorption as previously described.

At the twilight of midnight, however, there is this distinction: having performed worship and offered the *argha*, one should dismiss the *jñānamaṇḍala* with "Oṃ vajra muḥ," dissolve the *samayamaṇḍala* into one's own *jñānabīja*, and resolve upon the non-manifest *saṃbodhicitta* before going to sleep.

In the same way, on subsequent days, being aroused by the exhortation of the goddesses' concert, one should perform everything as before. Thus, every day until the signs of accomplishment (*siddhinimitta*) are obtained.
In that regard, the mantra of the Lord of the Maṇḍala is accomplished by one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajāpa*), while for the others, it is by ten thousand recitations (*ayutajāpa*).

The *mālāmantras* are to be brought from other tantras. Having formed them into a circle—either on the sun at one's own heart or on the moon at the heart, as appropriate—and having visualized them with the mind as blazing like a row of lamps, one should recite them while mentally repeating them as if they were being uttered by speech.
By the merit I have acquired through thus explaining this *mahāmāyā* sādhana,
may I become a Buddha, a master in accomplishing the welfare of all beings.
The *Mahāmāyāsādhana* is completed.
